title: Developer Productivity & Operational Enablement
intro: This domain covers how an architect makes AI tooling genuinely useful to engineering teams: configuring tools like Claude Code for consistent, safe team-wide use; improving real developer workflows rather than mandating tool usage; and applying AI safely to debugging and operational incident work. The exam tests judgment through scenarios — expect questions where the tempting answer is a tool-first mandate, a vanity metric, or an unverified AI suggestion, and the correct answer is the disciplined workflow-level choice.

objectives.objective: Configure Claude tools and environments for teams (e.g., Claude Code)
objectives.explanation:
Configuring Claude Code for a team is fundamentally about moving knowledge and policy out of individual developers' heads and into version-controlled artifacts the tool reads automatically. The central pieces are: CLAUDE.md, a project memory file checked into the repository that supplies conventions, build commands, architecture notes, and constraints to every session; settings.json, which splits into shared project settings (committed, applied to everyone) and user settings (personal preferences); hooks, which run deterministic commands at defined points in the agent's tool use, such as formatting after edits or blocking disallowed actions; custom slash commands and Skills, which package repeatable workflows; and MCP servers, which connect the agent to internal systems like ticket trackers, API catalogs, and documentation portals.

The key architectural distinction is between probabilistic and deterministic mechanisms. Instructions in CLAUDE.md or a prompt raise the likelihood of a behavior but never guarantee it; hooks and permission rules execute every time. An architect places each requirement on the right side of that line: style preferences and conventions belong in memory files, while must-happen behaviors (lint before finishing, never read .env, never run destructive commands without approval) belong in hooks and permission allowlists or denylists.

Permission policy is an access-control decision, and for sensitive repositories it follows least privilege: deny reads of secrets paths, allowlist known-safe commands, and prompt for approval on everything else. Crucially, this policy lives in shared project settings so the security posture of a repository does not depend on which developer opened it. Leaving permissions to individual configuration guarantees drift, and drift in a payments or patient-data repo is a security incident waiting to happen.
objectives.whyItMatters: In production organizations, per-developer configuration drift is the silent killer of AI tooling programs: the agent behaves differently on every laptop, new hires inherit whatever setup they pair on, and one loosely configured environment can expose secrets or damage shared infrastructure. Teams that treat agent configuration as versioned, reviewed engineering artifacts get consistent behavior, deterministic onboarding, and a defensible security posture; teams that don't accumulate incidents and lose trust in the tooling.

examples.title: Standardizing a monorepo shared by three squads
examples.body: Three squads share a monorepo, each with private prompt snippets and personal permission settings. After an agent with loose permissions modifies a shared CI script, the architect commits a baseline: a CLAUDE.md documenting build commands and conventions, a project settings.json with deny rules for .env and CI paths plus an allowlist of safe commands, and slash commands for the squads' common tasks. Personal settings remain only for genuinely individual preferences like editor integration. Onboarding drops from days of tribal knowledge to cloning the repo, and the incident class disappears because policy is now enforced by the tool, not by memory.

examples.title: Choosing a hook over a stronger instruction
examples.body: A team's CLAUDE.md says 'always run the formatter before finishing,' yet unformatted diffs still reach CI a few times a week. The architect recognizes that prompts are probabilistic: better wording raises compliance but cannot reach 100%. Because formatting is a must-happen behavior, the right mechanism is a post-edit hook that runs the formatter and linter automatically and blocks on failure. The instruction stays in CLAUDE.md as context, but enforcement moves to the deterministic layer — and the failure mode is eliminated rather than made rarer.

pitfalls: Relying on prompt instructions for behaviors that must happen every time — prompts are probabilistic, so guaranteed behaviors need hooks or permission rules instead.
Letting each developer manage their own permission settings on sensitive repositories, which makes the security posture depend on whose laptop is open rather than on team policy.
Treating CLAUDE.md as a dumping ground for everything — bloated memory files consume context in every session; stable conventions belong there, while live external data belongs behind MCP servers.
Documenting standards in a wiki instead of encoding them in version-controlled configuration, which codifies drift rather than eliminating it because nothing enforces what the wiki says.

Forgetting secrets hygiene — an agent that can freely read .env files or credentials directories will eventually surface them in output; deny rules for secrets paths should be in shared settings from day one.

objectives.objective: Improve developer workflows using AI-assisted tooling
objectives.explanation:
The discipline this objective tests is workflow-first adoption: start from the team's actual delivery constraints — code review latency, test debt, slow onboarding, documentation rot — and apply AI tooling where it relieves the bottleneck, rather than mandating tool usage and hoping value appears. Theory-of-constraints reasoning applies directly: accelerating code generation when review is the bottleneck just deepens the review queue. The high-value applications are usually AI-assisted first-pass code review, test generation against untested code, refactoring support, documentation generation, and helping engineers navigate unfamiliar codebases.

Measurement separates credible programs from checkbox rollouts. Vanity metrics — adoption percentage, lines of AI-generated code, prompt volume, even acceptance rate — measure tool activity, not delivery outcomes, and they can all rise while the organization ships no faster. The metrics that matter are cycle time, PR throughput, change-failure rate, and developer satisfaction, always compared against a baseline captured before the rollout. A managed rollout makes this possible: pilot with a real team on real backlog work, publish usage guidelines, measure for a defined period, then expand on evidence.

Two further practices make gains durable. First, capture proven workflows as executable artifacts: refined prompts and multi-step procedures become custom slash commands and Skills checked into the repo, so the best-known method is the default method and survives team churn. Second, preserve human accountability: the engineer who merges a change owns it, must be able to explain it, and reviews AI-authored diffs to the same standard as human-written ones. Velocity gains that come from rubber-stamping AI output are borrowed against future incidents.
objectives.whyItMatters: Organizations routinely spend heavily on AI developer tooling and cannot show delivery improvement, because they mandated tools instead of fixing workflows and measured usage instead of outcomes. Worse, teams that let review discipline erode ship AI-authored defects to production and then face pressure to ban the tooling entirely. The architect's job is to make the gains real (targeted at bottlenecks), provable (baselined outcome metrics), and safe (human accountability intact).

examples.title: Redirecting a 100%-adoption mandate
examples.body: A CTO mandates daily AI tool usage for all engineers. The architect's pipeline analysis shows coding is not the constraint — PRs wait a median of 2.5 days for review. Rather than pushing adoption metrics, the architect pilots AI-assisted first-pass review on two teams: the agent summarizes diffs, flags likely defects, and drafts review comments for the human reviewer to accept or reject. PR wait time drops measurably against the baseline, reviewers report less drudgery, and the demonstrated win drives voluntary adoption across other teams — the mandate becomes unnecessary because the tooling is now solving a felt problem.

examples.title: Turning prompt folklore into Skills
examples.body: One senior engineer gets excellent migration scripts from a carefully refined prompt; everyone else gets mediocre results from ad-hoc attempts, and the refined prompt lives in her personal notes. The architect has the workflow packaged as a custom slash command checked into the repo, with the procedure and safety checks encoded. Now any developer invokes the same proven workflow directly in Claude Code, improvements land through normal code review, and when the author changes teams the capability stays. Individual expertise has become organizational capability.

pitfalls: Tool-first rollouts — mandating adoption without identifying which workflow bottleneck the tool should relieve produces shallow usage and no delivery improvement.
Reporting vanity metrics like adoption percentage or AI-generated lines of code as impact; they measure activity, not outcomes, and can rise while delivery gets worse.
Skipping the baseline — without pre-adoption measurements of cycle time and throughput, even a successful program cannot demonstrate improvement.
Letting reviewers rubber-stamp AI-authored changes on the assumption the agent already checked them; accountability for merged code must stay with a named human.
Leaving proven prompts and workflows in personal notes or wikis instead of encoding them as shared slash commands and Skills, so the knowledge walks out the door with its author.

objectives.objective: Support debugging and operational issue resolution
objectives.explanation:
AI assistants are genuinely strong at the investigative side of operations: analyzing large volumes of logs, correlating metrics, explaining unfamiliar service code to an on-call engineer, and proposing hypotheses about root causes. The architectural question is how to grant that value safely. The standard answer splits permissions along the observe/act boundary: read-only access to logs, metrics, traces, and code carries minimal blast radius and can be granted freely for diagnosis, while any state-changing action — restarts, config edits, deployments — requires explicit human approval. Mid-incident is when human oversight is most rushed, which is exactly why the write path needs a deterministic gate rather than reliance on supervision.

Two verification disciplines keep AI-assisted debugging safe. First, a coherent explanation is not evidence: models produce fluent, confident analyses that are sometimes wrong. Before an AI-suggested fix reaches production, reproduce the failure with a test, confirm the patch makes that test pass, and run the existing suite — verify against the system's behavior, not the quality of the prose. Second, learn the signature of a guessing model: serially revised root causes, each authoritative-sounding, with shifting citations and no confirmed checks. When that pattern appears, the right move is to stop the AI-led thread and escalate to humans with real system context, handing over the hypotheses already eliminated so the time spent still adds value.

Beyond interactive incident work, Claude Code runs headless for programmatic use, which enables runbook automation: an alerting pipeline can trigger a headless invocation with a scoped prompt per alert class, read-only diagnostic permissions, and structured output posted to the incident channel. The design principle is deterministic triggering and guardrails around a model doing the interpretive work — the pipeline decides when to run and what the agent may touch; the model does the log-reading and summarizing that scripts cannot.
objectives.whyItMatters: Incidents are where the stakes of AI assistance are highest: a confidently wrong suggestion executed against production can turn one outage into two, and an engineer who cannot tell investigation from guessing burns the incident clock in a loop. Teams with clear guardrails — read-only diagnosis, approval-gated actions, test-verified fixes, and known escalation triggers — get faster triage without new failure modes; teams without them eventually have an incident caused by the tool meant to resolve incidents.

examples.title: Designing incident-response access for a payments platform
examples.body: A fintech team wants on-call engineers to use an AI assistant during payment-platform incidents, and the security lead fears production damage. The architect rejects both extremes — full engineer-equivalent permissions (supervision is weakest under incident stress) and staging-only access (staging lacks the live state that characterizes the incident). Instead the assistant gets read-only access to production logs, metrics, and code, with every state-changing action routed through explicit human approval. Diagnosis, the bulk of the work, flows freely; the rare risky action gets a deterministic gate.

examples.title: The patch that looked right
examples.body: During a checkout outage, Claude Code identifies a plausible race condition and produces a clean patch, and the incident commander pushes to deploy immediately. The engineer instead spends fifteen minutes writing a test that reproduces the failure, confirms the patch makes it pass, and runs the suite. In this case the fix was correct and the delay was small — but the same discipline is what catches the cases where the fluent explanation is wrong, and it prevents converting one outage into two. Plausibility never substitutes for verification.

pitfalls: Granting an incident assistant the on-call engineer's full write permissions because 'a human supervises every step' — incident pressure is precisely when supervision is least reliable.
Deploying an AI-suggested fix because the explanation is coherent; fluency is not evidence, and only a reproducing test plus the existing suite verifies the fix.
Treating the model's confidence as calibrated — asking it to rank its own hypotheses by confidence structures the guessing without adding any ground truth.
Failing to recognize the guessing signature (serially revised, authoritative root causes with shifting evidence) and continuing to feed the loop instead of escalating to humans.
Restricting AI diagnosis to staging to avoid production risk, which discards the live logs and state the investigation actually needs; the safe alternative is read-only production access.
